title: Calling the name
hookLine: Namu Amida Butsu in Japan, Namo Amituofo in China

lines: SAID OVER RICE, IN A CORRIDOR, IN A HOSPITAL BED.
cards: In a temple in Kyoto, a room full of voices: Namu Amida Butsu. In a temple in Taipei or Singapore, the same name in another tongue: Namo Amituofo. A grandmother says it over her rice.
A monk says it as he passes you in a corridor. A man in a hospital bed says it under his breath when the pain comes. The sutra's pictures take patience.
This practice can be done by anyone with a voice, or just the breath to whisper. Today's word is the name, said aloud: nembutsu.

teach.b: First, the name, which you met in year three with Honen. Namu Amida Butsu and Namo Amituofo are one phrase in two languages.

teach.h: NAMU: A BOW. AMIDA: INFINITE LIGHT.
teach.b: Amida and Amituofo are both Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light. Namu, or namo, is a word of bowing: homage, turning toward, taking refuge. So the whole phrase is a bow, made of sound.
Second, the word nembutsu. It's usually rendered as keeping the Buddha in mind.
In Pure Land practice, keeping the Buddha in mind came to include saying his name aloud; thinking and saying grew close enough to share a word. Third, the passage that makes this practice so plain.
Near the end of the Contemplation Sutra, the Buddha describes a person who has done much wrong in life and comes to the hour of death in fear and pain.

teach.h: IF YOU CANNOT PICTURE HIM, SAY HIS NAME.
teach.b: A good friend sits beside him and tries to teach him to picture the Buddha, but he can't; he is too pressed by suffering to hold any picture at all.

teach.h: WITHIN REACH ON THE WORST DAY.
teach.b: So the friend says, in effect: if you cannot think of him, just say his name.
The sutra says he calls the name ten times, and is born in the land of bliss. Fourth, why that matters. The pictures need a steady mind.
The name is offered to the person who has none left. Pure Land teachers who put it at the heart of the path point to this passage: it is within reach on the worst day as on the best.

how: Pure Land Buddhists say the nembutsu aloud in temple services, quietly in daily life, and with prayer beads to keep count; Japanese practitioners say Namu Amida Butsu, and Chinese practitioners Namo Amituofo.

o: a monk's vow to recite one sutra every day
keeping the Buddha in mind, and calling his name
a silent breath count used before Zen sitting

games.q: calling the name: tap the pairs.
p: a word of bowing, taking refuge

s: Namu Amida Butsu and Namo Amituofo are two different practices
they're one phrase in two languages, both bowing to Amitabha.
in the sutra, the dying man can't picture the Buddha
he is too pressed by suffering, so the friend tells him to say the name instead.
the name is only for people with a steady mind
in the sutra it is offered to the person who has no steady mind left.

games.q: you're the good friend at a dying man's side. you try to teach him to picture the Buddha, but he's in too much pain to hold any picture. what do you do?
o: keep explaining the picture until he gets it.
tell him: if you cannot think of him, just say his name.
let him rest and say nothing.
games.why: the friend tells him to just say the name. the sutra says he calls it ten times and is born in the land of bliss.

practice: If you'd like, say Namu Amida Butsu or Namo Amituofo slowly, once with each out-breath, ten times, aloud or under your breath, counting on your fingers if that helps.
If you'd rather not say it, listen to the sound of it in your mind, as a word from a tradition you're visiting. After the tenth, sit quietly with whatever is left.

wordCard.voice: Nembutsu. Keeping the Buddha in mind, and in Pure Land practice, calling his name: Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: nembutsu, keeping the Buddha in mind; in Pure Land practice, calling Amida's name.

carryVoice: Your line: just the name. When the pictures won't come, the name still can. Rest well.

sources.ref: Amitayur-dhyana Sutra, the sixteenth contemplation (the lowest grade of birth)

sources.work: Pure Land communal practice, Japan and China
